DS256: Scalability Analysis of an LLM Data

Preprocessing Pipeline with PySpark

Yuvaraj DC

yuvarajdc@iisc.ac.in

Chethan

chethan1@iisc.ac.in

March 10, 2026

Abstract

This report presents a comprehensive scalability analysis of a real-world Large Language

Model (LLM) data preprocessing pipeline implemented in PySpark. The pipeline ingests raw

Common Crawl data (WARC files) and processes it through six stages: WARC-to-Parquet

conversion, domain-based filtering, text extraction with Trafilatura, language identification

with FastText, near-duplicate deduplication (MinHash LSH), and tokenization. We conduct

three distinct studies: (1) strong scaling, where we fix the dataset and increase computational

resources; (2) weak scaling, where we proportionally increase both data size and resources;

and (3) memory sensitivity, where we analyze the impact of varying executor memory. Our

results indicate that the pipeline scales effectively up to 64 cores for a fixed 7.8 GB dataset,

after which communication overhead dominates. For weak scaling, configurations with 4

cores per executor significantly outperform those with 2 cores.

The memory sensitivity

study reveals that 8 GB per executor is optimal for a 31 GB dataset, minimizing costly disk

spill and garbage collection overhead. All data and visualizations presented are derived from

the accompanying Jupyter notebook, figure table plotting.ipynb.

1

Introduction and Pipeline Overview

The objective of this study is to analyze the scalability and performance characteristics of a

real-world Large Language Model (LLM) data preprocessing pipeline implemented in PySpark.

The pipeline, detailed in the code file a1 v1.0.py, processes raw web crawl data (WARC files)

through a series of six stages to produce clean, tokenized training data.

The goal of this report is to provide a detailed analysis of the pipeline’s behavior under

different resource configurations.

We will evaluate its strong scaling performance, its weak

scaling performance, and its sensitivity to executor memory allocations. All data presented in

this report is derived from the figure table plotting.ipynb notebook.

1.1

Pipeline Stages

The LLM preprocessing pipeline consists of six distinct stages, each performing a specific trans-

formation on the data. The logic and resource consumption of each stage contribute uniquely

to the overall scaling characteristics observed in the experiments.

• Step 1: WARC to Parquet Conversion (Ingestion & Parsing): The raw input

data consists of .warc files stored on HDFS. This stage lists these files and processes them

in parallel using a Spark RDD flatMap operation. For each record within a WARC file, it

filters for response records containing HTML content and parses the headers and content.

The output is a structured DataFrame, which is then written to HDFS in the efficient

Parquet format, partitioned by the source filename. This stage is primarily I/O-bound

and involves parsing unstructured data.

• Step 2: Domain Filtering: The pipeline ingests the Parquet data and filters out records

originating from a predefined blacklist of domains. It loads a list of blacklisted domains

from HDFS and broadcasts it to all executors for efficient lookups. The core of the logic

involves extracting the host from the URL, generating all possible parent domains (e.g.,

sub.example.com -> example.com), and performing a broadcast join against the blacklist

to identify and remove unwanted records. This stage is CPU-bound for domain extraction

and network/shuffle-bound for the join operation.

• Step 3: Text Extraction with Trafilatura: The raw HTML content from the filtered

records is passed to the trafilatura library. This library performs complex parsing to

extract clean, readable main text content, stripping away boilerplate, ads, and naviga-

tion menus. This is a highly CPU-intensive operation, executed as a user-defined func-

tion (UDF) over the DataFrame. The performance of this stage is highly dependent on

the complexity of the HTML and is typically the computational bottleneck of the entire

pipeline.

• Step 4:

Language Identification (FastText):

The extracted text is fed into a

fasttext language identification model to detect its language. The model, a pre-trained

binary file distributed to nodes via Spark’s file management, predicts the language for each

document. Only documents classified as English with a probability above a threshold (de-

fault 0.6) are retained. Like Step 3, this stage involves a UDF and is computationally

expensive, but it is generally faster than the text extraction step. The fasttext model

is loaded once per executor, which is a key optimization.

• Step 5: Deduplication: This stage employs two methods to remove duplicate content,

as studied in the experiments:

– 5a. Near-Duplicate Deduplication (MinHash LSH): To remove near-duplicate

documents (e.g., articles that are very similar but not identical), the pipeline uses

3

Spark MLlib’s MinHashLSH. It converts text into character 5-grams, hashes them,

and generates MinHash signatures.

An LSH model is then used to find pairs of

documents with a Jaccard distance less than or equal to 0.5. From each cluster of

similar documents, only the longest one is kept. This process involves significant

computation for feature extraction and a large, shuffle-heavy self-join to find similar

pairs.

– 5b. Exact Deduplication (MD5): This simpler method calculates an MD5 hash

of the entire extracted text.

Records with duplicate MD5 hashes are considered

identical, and only one copy (the earliest by date) is retained. This is a lightweight

operation compared to MinHash LSH, requiring minimal computation and shuffle.

• Step 6: Tokenization: The final stage converts the cleaned text into fixed-length token

sequences suitable for LLM training. It tokenizes the text using a regex word-boundary

pattern, maps each word to a token ID using a hashing function (bounded by a vocabulary

size), and then either truncates or pads the sequence to a maximum length of 512 tokens.

An attention mask is generated to distinguish real tokens from padding. This is a CPU-

bound stage executed via a UDF.

4

2

Experimental Setup

All experiments were conducted on a dedicated YARN cluster. The cluster configuration and

experiment methodology are as follows:

• Cluster Hardware: 8 nodes, each with 72 vcores (hyper-threaded) and 128 GiB of RAM.

• YARN Queue: Jobs were submitted to a dedicated team queue (root.ds256.team8)

with a guaranteed capacity of 8.33% of the cluster, which could expand to a maximum of

25%.

• Spark Configuration (Baseline):

– Executor Memory Overhead: Set to 2GB unless overridden in the memory sen-

sitivity study.

– Metrics: spark.executor.processTreeMetrics.enabled and

spark.eventLog.logStageExecutorMetrics were enabled to capture detailed per-

formance data, which was processed by scripts/extract metrics.py to produce

the metrics in the final data.csv file.

• Data Sets: The input data consisted of six datasets of varying sizes, named small X,

with the following sizes in GB:

– small 1: 3.9 GB

– small 2: 7.8 GB

– small 4: 15.7 GB

– small 6: 23.4 GB

– small 8: 31.0 GB

– small 16: 62.2 GB

• Experiment Methodology: Each configuration was run multiple times (iterations=3)

to account for runtime variability. A 10-second cool-down period was enforced between

runs to allow for cluster cleanup. Key metrics such as stage times, total execution time,

and deep JVM metrics (GC, shuffle, compute ratios) were captured for each run. More

information about the metrics used is provided in the Appendix.

Strong Scaling Analysis

Strong scaling measures how the total execution time of the pipeline decreases as we add more

computational resources (number of executors keeping fixed cores per executors) while keeping

the problem size (dataset) constant. For this experiment, we fixed the dataset at small 2 (7.8

GB) and varied the number of executors while keeping each executor configured with 8 GB of

memory and 4 cores. So the total cores will be thr product of number of executor and the

cores per executor. All timings are reported in seconds, and data, memory, and disk sizes are

reported in GB.

The pipeline demonstrates strong scaling, with execution time decreasing from ≈1009 seconds

on 8 cores to ≈336 seconds on 64 cores (Figure 1a). However, the scaling is far from ideal. As

shown in Table 1 and Figure 1b, speedup plateaus after 64 cores despite doubling the hardware

resources. The maximum measured speedup is 2.97×, far below the ideal 16×.

3.1.1

Applying Amdahl’s Law confirms this observation:

Where f represents the serial fraction of the pipeline. This analysis reveals that 33% of the

pipeline is inherently serial (the non-parallelizable fraction f), which caps the maximum

achievable speedup at 1/f = 3× regardless of how many cores are added. for this dataset size.

The theoretical minimum runtime is 1010/3 ≈337 seconds, which matches our observed runtime

at 64+ cores. Error bars are largest at low core counts (8-16), reflecting YARN scheduling non-

determinism when few tasks are in-flight.

3.1.2

Parallel Efficiency

Efficiency E = S(N)/N measures how effectively added cores are utilized. Table 1 and Figure

2 show a steep and continuous decline. The steepest drop (99% →48%) occurs between 8 and

32 cores, after which the decline continues more gradually. Beyond 64 cores, each additional

core delivers practically no improvement – hardware resources are effectively wasted.

The optimal operating region lies between 32 and 64 cores, where absolute execution time

is meaningfully reduced (from 519s to 336s) while maintaining acceptable efficiency above 37%.

The efficiency, which measures how effectively added cores are utilized, drops significantly from

63.9% at 16 cores to just 18.3% at 128 cores (Figure 2). This indicates that for this 7.8 GB

dataset, the optimal resource allocation is around 64 cores. Beyond this point, the overhead

of task scheduling, coordination, and diminishing returns from task parallelism outweigh the

benefits of adding more cores.

Figure 3 is the most revealing strong scaling result. Observations per stage:

• S1 (WARC Parsing): The time remains constant almost because each executor is

• S2 (Domain filtering): Since we are handling the fixed sized restricted domains is

taking almost .

• S3 (Trafilatura): Scales from ≈175 s →49 s at 64 cores (3.6×). Embarrassingly parallel

via mapPartitions no inter-task communication.

• S4 (FastText): Best-scaling stage, 5× improvement (160 s →32 s). The executor-level

model singleton (one lid.176.bin load per executor process) eliminates repeated I/O

overhead.

• S5a (MinHash LSH): The critical bottleneck. Starts largest at ≈200 s, scales to ≈47 s

at 64 cores, then stops improving at 128 cores. The approxSimilarityJoin self-

join shuffles candidate pairs across all executor pairs – communication cost grows with

executor count, eventually canceling compute gains.

• S5b (MD5 Dedup): Scales 20× (160 s →8 s). dropDuplicates on a hash column is a

clean shuffle-sort with no quadratic growth.

• S6a & S6b (Tokenization): This step also scales well as it involves tokenization and

computing attention mask which scales well.

A deeper look at the resource ratios (Table 3, Figure 4a) reveals the primary bottleneck. As

the number of cores scales up, the ”Communication Ratio” increases dramatically from a negli-

gible 0.51% at 8 cores to 8.55% at 128 cores. This is a classic symptom of Amdahl’s Law, where

the serial portion of the workload (in this case, the need to shuffle data for operations like the

LSH self-join) begins to dominate. The rising communication ratio directly explains efficiency

loss: at 128 cores, 1 in 10 executor-seconds is spent on inter-node shuffle, not computation.

Concurrently, the ”Compute Ratio” decreases.

The results in Table 5 and Figure 5a clearly show that using 4 cores per executor yields signif-

icantly better performance than 2 cores. The execution time for the largest dataset (31 GB)

is 1206 seconds with 4-core executors, compared to 2369 seconds with 2-core executors. This

indicates that the pipeline benefits from more powerful executors that can handle more of the

computational workload within a single JVM, reducing inter-executor communication.

However, the weak scaling is not perfect for either configuration.

The time per unit of

data (Figure 5b) shows a general upward trend, especially for the 2-core executor configuration,

confirming that overhead increases with the scale of the job. The 4-core configuration, while

faster, also shows a noticeable increase in execution time as data grows, particularly at the

32-core/15.7 GB point.

4.2

Execution Time & Normalized Throughput

Neither configuration achieves flat weak scaling (Figure 5a). The 2-cores/executor configuration

rises from ≈1,878 s (2 cores, small 1) to ≈2,902 s (32 cores, small 16) – a 55% increase for

16× data. The 4-cores/executor configuration rises sharply to ≈1,302 s at 32 cores, then par-

tially recovers and stabilizes at ≈1,200 s at 48–64 cores. This stabilization reflects intra-executor

parallelism compensating for inter-executor coordination at larger scales. The 4-cores/executor

is consistently ≈2× faster at equivalent core counts: at 32 cores it uses 8 executors vs. 16,

halving YARN coordination traffic. Executor count drives the performance gap, not total core

count.

Figure 5b: time-per-unit-data declines steeply, appearing superlinear. This is an artifact of

high fixed startup costs (YARN launch, FastText model load, SparkSession init) being amortized

over larger datasets. True per-byte cost converges to ≈165–195 s/unit at large scale.

Figure 6 shows which stages break weak scaling:

• S5a – primary violator.

Consistently the tallest bars, with dramatic irregularity:

≈500 s at 12 cores, ≈450 s at 32 cores. As data doubles, LSH candidate pairs grow faster

than 2×, triggering spill cascades and high run-to-run variance.

• S3 & S4 – favorable. Both decline under 4-cores/executor at scale. Larger partitions are

handled faster by more intra-executor cores; CPU-bound embarrassingly parallel stages

genuinely benefit.

• S2 – near-ideal.

Bars stay flat at ≈20–25 s.

One anomalous spike at 32 cores (2-

cores/exec) suggests YARN scheduling contention at peak executor count.

• S5b – near-linear. Grows moderately then declines to ≈155 s at 64 cores – a stark

contrast to S5a’s super-linear growth.

4.4

Shuffle Growth & Parallelism Utilization

(a) Shuffle read explodes to 3,450 s at 64 cores (4-

cores/exec). Write stays flat <100 s throughout.

(b) Parallelism grows linearly – Spark fully utilizes

all cores. The bottleneck is coordination overhead,

not task count.

Figure 7: Weak scaling – shuffle time growth and parallelism utilization.

Figure 7a: shuffle read explodes super-linearly, reaching ≈3,436 s at 64 cores (4-cores/exec)

– larger than the entire pipeline at small scales.

Shuffle write stays flat (<100 s) in both

configurations, confirming the bottleneck is the read-side sort-merge of MinHash LSH

hash buckets, not the write phase. This is the single most important scalability finding: S5a’s

shuffle read will dominate the pipeline at production-scale datasets.

Figure 7b: parallelism grows linearly with total cores for both configurations – Spark’s

task scheduler fully utilizes all available resources. The performance problem is coordination

overhead and algorithmic complexity, not under-utilization or insufficient task count.

4.5

Resource Contention and Spill

A key observation from the weak scaling experiment is the relationship between data size and

memory spill. As shown in Figure 8a, the amount of memory spill increases almost linearly

with the dataset size. With the fixed 8GB per executor, larger datasets force Spark to spill

more intermediate data to disk, which is a major contributor to the increase in execution time.

This effect is less pronounced for the 4-core executors, as they can process their larger share of

data more efficiently within their memory space. The 2-cores/executor configuration maintains

≈98–99% compute ratio even as performance degrades – an artifact where disk spill I/O time is

counted as compute, masking the true bottleneck. The 4-cores/executor configuration honestly

shows compute declining to ≈90% and communication rising to ≈9% at 64 cores, mirroring the

strong scaling pattern.

The 4-core executor configuration also shows a lower and more stable time per unit data (Fig-

ure 5b), suggesting it is a more efficient and scalable choice for this pipeline. The performance

of the 2-core configuration degrades more rapidly, highlighting that for a compute-intensive

pipeline, having more cores per executor is beneficial.

memory spill grows from ≈4 GB to

≈32 GB for 2-cores/executor – an 8× increase for 16× data – confirming super-linear growth.

The 4-cores/executor configuration is more moderate, reaching ≈23.5 GB at 64 cores.

The

crossover where 4-cores/executor is strictly better on all memory metrics occurs at ≈15–16

total cores.

4.6

Compute vs. Communication Trade-off

Figure 9 illustrates how the allocation of resources impacts the nature of the work being done.

At very low memory (2GB), the pipeline is forced to spill data to disk, a process that consumes

both I/O and CPU, but the relative ”Communication Ratio” (shuffle) is low. As memory in-

creases and spill decreases, tasks can hold more data in memory and perform more computation

efficiently, leading to a higher ”Compute Ratio”. The ”Communication Ratio” remains rela-

tively stable but increases slightly with higher memory, likely because more data is successfully

passed through shuffle stages without being spilled, but the shuffle itself is still a bottleneck.

This analysis reveals that 8GB is the ”sweet spot” for this configuration, balancing the need to

avoid spill against the diminishing returns and potential overhead of a larger heap.

Memory Sensitivity Study

This study investigates how executor memory allocation affects pipeline performance and re-

source consumption. Experiments ran on small 8 (31 GB) with 16 executors and 2 cores each,

varying executor memory from 2 GB to 10 GB.

5.1

The Spill Paradox

(a) Average memory components across all exper-

iments. Memory spill (11.7 GB) is 4.5× the peak

heap (2.6 GB).

(b) Peak heap distribution by scaling type. Me-

dians are within 0.1 GB of each other across all

experiment types.

Figure 10: Memory profile overview across all experiments.

Figure 10a highlights a significant disparity between peak heap usage and total memory spill.

The average memory spill (11.7 GB) is 4.5× the peak heap (2.6 GB). An executor whose

working set needs only 2.6 GB generates 4.5× that volume in shuffle intermediate data. This

is caused by the MinHash LSH self-join in S5a generating candidate pairs that overflow shuffle

buffers – a structural property of the algorithm, not a tuning problem. No amount of

increasing executor heap can eliminate it.

Figure 10b shows that peak heap is invariant at ≈2.7 GB median across strong scaling,

weak scaling, and memory study experiments – despite wildly different data sizes and executor

counts. Peak heap remains at approximately 2.7 GB across all configurations, suggesting the

working set is insensitive to executor count and data size. allocating more than ≈3 GB of heap

per executor yields no benefit to the working set.

15

5.2

Execution Time and Spill Behavior

(a) Execution time vs. executor memory. Time in-

creases beyond 6 GB due to YARN container sizing

and larger shuffle buffer overhead.

(b) Memory and disk spill vs. executor memory.

Spill decreases only 19% from 4 GB to 8 GB – ir-

reducible with the current S5a design.

Figure 11: Memory sensitivity – execution time and spill vs. executor memory.

Figure 11a shows that execution time improves from 2 GB (≈1,550 s) to 6 GB (≈1,350 s), after

which it increases to ≈2,080 s at 8 GB and degrades further at 10 GB. Two mechanisms explain

the counter-intuitive rise: (1) larger YARN containers take longer to schedule on the cluster;

(2) larger Spark shuffle buffers increase total data written during sort-merge before spilling,

paradoxically generating more intermediate work. The widening error bars at higher memory

values confirm non-deterministic YARN placement behaviour. 6–8 GB is the practical sweet

spot beyond which additional memory hurts more than it helps.

Figure 11b directly explains the execution time trend. At 2 GB and 4 GB, executor memory

is insufficient to hold shuffle buffers for S5a’s self-join and S2’s domain filter join, forcing large

amounts of data to spill to disk. Memory spill drops steeply from 2 GB to 6 GB, after which

the reduction becomes marginal – only 19% less spill when doubling from 4 GB to 8 GB. Spill

never reaches zero at any tested value, confirming it is structurally irreducible with the current

MinHash LSH implementation.

5.3

Peak Heap and GC Overhead

(a) Peak heap usage vs. executor memory. Heap

declines only 140 MB across the full 4–8 GB range;

>5 GB sits unused at 8 GB allocation.

(b) GC ratio vs. executor memory. GC drops from

1.75% to 1.05% – a real improvement but inconse-

quential since GC is <2% of total executor time.

Figure 12: Memory sensitivity – heap usage and GC overhead vs. executor memory.

16

Figure 12a confirms that the pipeline’s working set is fixed at ≈2.7 GB regardless of allocation.

Peak heap declines only trivially from 2,843 MB (4 GB) to 2,703 MB (8 GB) – a 140 MB drop

despite doubling the allocation.

At 8 GB per executor, over 5 GB of allocated memory sits

completely unused. This rules out heap pressure as the cause of spill entirely.

Figure 12b shows GC ratio declining monotonically from 1.75% at 4 GB to 1.05% at 8 GB.

While the trend is clean and expected – more headroom means fewer GC cycles – the absolute

values are too small (<2% of total executor time) to have any material impact on pipeline

performance. GC is not a bottleneck at any tested memory configuration.

5.4

Spill–Heap Decoupling & Cross-Experiment GC Patterns

(a) Memory spill vs. peak heap across all exper-

iments. No correlation – high-spill and low-spill

points appear at identical heap values.

(b) GC time vs. memory spill across all experiment

types. Weak scaling shows non-linear GC growth

beyond 15 GB – a self-reinforcing spill–GC feed-

back loop.

Figure 13: Cross-experiment memory characterization.

Figure 13a provides the definitive proof that peak heap and memory spill are completely

independent quantities. High-spill points (30+ GB) appear at the same peak heap values

(2.2–2.6 GB) as near-zero-spill points. The large yellow bubbles (128 cores, strong scaling) have

the highest heap (≈2.85 GB) yet the lowest spill (≈4 GB). Increasing heap allocation cannot

reduce spill – they are driven by entirely different mechanisms: heap by partition size, spill by

S5a shuffle volume.

Figure 13b reveals three distinct behavioural clusters across experiment types.

Strong

scaling (pink) groups tightly at low spill (≈4 GB) with GC 140–290 s – fixed data keeps both

metrics bounded and stable. Weak scaling (gold) spans the full range, with GC growing

non-linearly beyond ≈15 GB of spill: high spill triggers more frequent full GC cycles, which

slow the shuffle phase, which causes more spill – a positive feedback effect between spill and

GC overhead. Memory study points (green) cluster at ≈23–24 GB spill with GC 405–620 s,

lower than comparable weak scaling points because fewer JVM instances (16 vs. up to 32) reduce

per-node GC contention.

17

5.5

Spill Growth with Dataset Size

(a) Spill by dataset under weak scaling. Memory

spill grows 32× for 16× data – super-linear growth

driven by S5a’s candidate pair explosion.

(b) Spill trends vs. total cores. The 2-cores/exec

configuration grows explosively to 32 GB at 32

cores; 4-cores/exec is more moderate.

Figure 14: Spill growth with dataset size under weak scaling.

Figure 14a quantifies how spill scales with raw data size.

Memory spill grows from ≈1 GB

(small 1, 3.9 GB) to ≈32 GB (small 16, 62.2 GB) – a 32× increase for only 16× data,

confirming super-linear growth. The memory-to-disk spill ratio stays consistently at ≈3:1 across

all dataset sizes, showing Spark uses ∼75% in-memory buffering before overflowing to disk. This

ratio being stable means the spill problem scales predictably but never goes away.

Figure 14b compares spill trends across the two executor configurations. The 2-cores/executor

curve (orange) grows nearly quadratically, reaching 32 GB at 32 cores. The 4-cores/executor

curve (green) grows more gradually to ≈23.5 GB at 64 cores despite processing twice the data

– because larger executors provide more shuffle buffer memory per task, delaying the onset of

spill. The crossover point where 4-cores/executor becomes strictly better on all memory metrics

occurs at ≈15–16 total cores.

6.3

Best Performance Configuration

Based on the strong scaling analysis, the best performance was achieved with 16 executors each

running with 4 cores (64 total cores). This configuration executed the 7.8 GB dataset in 316.07

seconds, offering the best trade-off between resource usage and execution time.

6.4

Most Efficient Configuration

The most efficient configuration, defined by the lowest time per core, was 32 executors with 4

cores each (128 total cores), with a time per core of 2.57 seconds. While this configuration was

only marginally faster than the 64-core setup, it demonstrates that for very large clusters, time

per core can remain low if the workload is sufficiently parallelizable.

For weak scaling, the most efficient configuration (lowest time per unit data) was 16 executors

with 4 cores each (64 total cores), processing the 31 GB dataset in 1205.86 seconds, with a time

per unit data of 147.82 seconds per size factor.

6.5

Configuration Recommendations

• Executor config: 4 cores/executor, 4–5 GB memory. Lowest coordination over-

head, adequate shuffle buffers, no wasted heap above the 2.7 GB working set.

• Core count: 32–64 total cores for datasets ≤30 GB. Efficiency is 37–48%. Beyond 64

cores, hardware is wasted for this workload.

• Memory: 4 GB/executor is optimal. More memory increases execution time (YARN

effects) while reducing spill by only ∼19%.

21

• Partitioning: Repartition to 200 after S1 WARC parsing. For datasets >30 GB, use

repartition(400+).

6.6

Algorithmic Redesign Priorities

1. S5a ReplaceapproxSimilarityJoin: Implement custom banding that hashes MinHash

signatures into band buckets and groups by bucket ID without a full self-join. Reduces

shuffle from O(n2) to O(n·b). Expected: 5–10× speedup at large scale.

2. S1 – Pre-split large WARC files: Split files >1 GB into ∼200 MB segments before

ingestion, enabling true file-level parallelism beyond WARC file count.

3. S3 – Apache Arrow Pandas UDFs: Replace mapPartitions with Arrow-based Pan-

das UDFs to eliminate JVM↔Python serialization.

Expected: 2–3× speedup for the

extraction stage.

22

7

Conclusion

This scalability study provides a detailed performance analysis of an LLM data preprocessing

pipeline. The key findings are:

1. Strong Scaling: The pipeline scales effectively up to 64 cores for a 7.8 GB dataset.

Beyond this point, communication overhead from shuffle-intensive operations (like the

domain filter join and deduplication) becomes the dominant bottleneck, limiting further

speedup. Strong scaling achieves 2.97× speedup (37% efficiency) at 64 cores before sat-

urating completely due to a 67% serial fraction dominated by S5a’s MinHash shuffle

overhead.

2. Weak Scaling: The pipeline handles increasing data sizes, but execution time does not

remain constant. Configurations with 4 cores per executor significantly outperform those

with 2 cores, demonstrating the benefit of more powerful executors for compute-intensive

workloads. Memory spill increases linearly with data size, contributing to performance

degradation. Weak scaling degrades 55% over 16× data scale-up, with shuffle read time

exploding to 3,450 s at 64 cores.

3. Memory Sensitivity: Allocating sufficient memory to executors is critical to minimize

performance-degrading disk spill and GC overhead. For a 31 GB dataset with 16 two-core

executors, 8 GB of memory per executor was found to be the optimal balance. Memory

spill (≈11.7 GB average) is structurally driven by the LSH self-join and is completely insen-

sitive to executor heap allocation – counter-intuitively, allocating more memory increases

execution time.

4. Recommendations: For jobs similar to this pipeline, we recommend:

• The recommended production configuration is 4 cores/executor, 4–5 GB mem-

ory, 8–16 executors for datasets under 32 GB. Scaling beyond that requires algo-

rithmic redesign of S5a – the pipeline’s single greatest obstacle to production-scale

deployment.

• Using executors with 4 cores, as they provide a better ratio of computational power

to memory.

• Allocating memory such that intermediate data can be held in memory to avoid spill,

with 8 GB per executor serving as a good baseline for similar data volumes.

• Recognizing that the pipeline’s scalability is limited by shuffle-heavy operations; fu-

ture optimization efforts should focus on minimizing shuffle in stages like domain

filtering and LSH-based deduplication.

Code & Scripts: https://github.com/ChethanPutran/SSDS

Appendix

This section provides detailed definitions for all metrics used in the scalability analysis of the

PySpark LLM preprocessing pipeline. These metrics are collected during pipeline execution

and used to evaluate performance, resource utilization, and scaling characteristics.

Core Configuration Metrics

Metric

Definition

Executors

Number of JVM processes launched to execute tasks.

Each executor runs on a node in the cluster and man-

ages resources for a set of tasks. Executors are launched

at the beginning of a Spark application and run for its

entire lifetime.

Cores per Executor

Number of CPU cores allocated to each executor. This

determines how many concurrent tasks each executor can

run simultaneously. Also known as executor cores or ex-

ecutor CPU slots.

Total Cores

Product of number of executors and cores per executor.

Represents the maximum parallel capacity of the cluster:

TotalCores = Executors × CoresPerExecutor

Dataset Size

Identifier for the input data size used in the experiment.

Common values: small 1, small 2, small 4 representing

relative data volumes. The numeric suffix indicates the

relative size factor.

Scenario

Type of scaling experiment performed:

• Strong Scaling: Fixed problem size, increasing re-

sources

• Weak Scaling: Problem size increases proportion-

ally with resources

• Memory Study: Fixed problem size and cores,

increasing memory
